analysis.summary_cn: Vercel 更新 Workflow SDK 至 5.2.0：事件写入与流写入默认改走 WebSocket，取代此前每次写入或每组流写入单独发一次 HTTP 请求，升级即生效、无需改代码。官方基准显示，回放 AI Agent token 流时完整响应交付快 4.2 倍，且没有分片延迟超过一秒；步骤开始与结束的事件写入也改走 WebSocket，多步骤工作流 HTTP 请求更少，性能与成本均改善。

raw_summary:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

Get started

Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide, since v5 is a major release.

Read more
title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.09061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.
title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.09085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.
title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed

arXiv:2611.09090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.
title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition

raw_summary:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

raw_summary:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember

Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.

The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output
GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75
Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50
>200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50
Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50

But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.

For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)

Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.

Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder, which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.09094v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.
title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs

raw_summary:
Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning.

Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. 

Beyond one workload, one nodepool 

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. 

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. 

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.  

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE 

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. 

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing 

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps 

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.

analysis.summary_cn: 该 arXiv 论文用 25 个 GPT-2-small 模型对比自然语言（TinyStories）与 Python、C、x86-64 汇编及机器码训练对大脑对齐度的影响。结果显示自然语言训练在 Pereira-243 和 Tuckute2024 基准上显著优于代码训练（Δr≈0.05），代码训练的对齐度接近随机权重；表征几何分析亦表明自然语言模型的神经相似度更高。结论：代码抽象无法替代自然语言训练带来的脑对齐表征几何。

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.09027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code-trained language models produce positive brain scores, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can substitute for natural-language training. We trained 25 GPT-2-small models on TinyStories, Python, C functions, x86-64 assembly, and the corresponding machine code, and scored them using a shared tokenizer and encoding procedure against matched random-weight models. On Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024, TinyStories exceeds the mean of the four code models by $\Delta r = 0.053$ and $0.059$ (Holm-corrected $p<0.001$), while code training leaves alignment near the random-weight level. The language advantage is benchmark-specific: Blank2014 shows no corrected language-code difference, and Fedorenko2016 shows no language benefit. Geometry tracks the encoding result on Pereira-243: TinyStories seeds converge on the most similar representations, and its fit-free correspondence with neural dissimilarity peaks at $\rho = 0.14$, twice the code and random-weight levels. Binary-trained models have about three effective dimensions, so seed agreement alone does not imply neural correspondence. Updating only the embedding matrix on English improves mean-over-depth alignment for every code model more than an equal update on its own corpus. Within this architecture and training setup, natural-language training produces a distinct representational geometry with closer neural correspondence on Pereira-243
title: Language, Not Code Abstraction: Natural-language Training Shapes Brain-aligned Geometry

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.09491v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models enable fine-tuning-free spoken language understanding (SLU) through in-context learning, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar yet intent irrelevant demonstrations. This paper presents Query-Adaptive Intent Detection via Prototype Extraction (APEX), a two-stage retrieval framework that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves contextual exemplars within the selected intent space. Experiments on the SLURP dataset evaluate joint SLU performance using Exact Match Accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, with additional retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts. Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B, respectively, on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs, APEX also yields EMA gains of 7.66 and 2.13 percentage points. Retrieval analysis further indicates that prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.
title: An Effective Spoken Language Understanding Approach Leveraging Query-Adaptive Intent Detection

raw_summary:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

raw_summary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

raw_summary:
Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia.

Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology.

To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve.

Legacy IT’s operational toll

In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions.

The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address.

This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems.

Enterprise monoculture

Why do organizations continue to rely on legacy environments that constrain their modernization? As our research shows, it is not necessarily architectural preference — but the result of vendor lock-in.
 
Beyond narrowing technology choice, deep provider dependence introduces commercial constraints. In our study, 39% of decision-makers report that reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them to navigate complex licensing rules or contracts, or limited negotiating flexibility.
 
Even more concerning is the systemic operational risk created by single-vendor concentration. Concentrating operating systems, productivity applications, cloud hosting and emerging AI models within a single vendor's monoculture creates an immense single point of failure. An autonomous AI agent is only as secure as the operating system and network it traverses. When that underlying stack is vulnerable, organizations are not deploying resilient intelligence; they are expanding their attack surface.

Customer choice

The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures.

Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software.

Accelerate agentic technology

Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there:

  • Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits.
  • Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches.
  • Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments.

The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running?
